title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:toxico

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Carcinogenicity. Lifetime rodent studies (18-24 months) for tumours: initiation, promotion, progression.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:toxico

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Genotoxicity battery. Ames test, in vitro mammalian cell assay, in vivo micronucleus test.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:toxico

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Repeated-dose studies. Subacute 28 days, subchronic 90 days, chronic 6 months to 2 years; define the NOAEL.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:toxico

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Reproductive toxicity. Fertility, embryo-fetal development (teratogenicity), pre/postnatal and multigeneration studies.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:toxico

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Single-dose studies. Acute toxicity: LD₅₀ or maximum tolerated dose, target organs, signs; animals watched 14 days.

title: Purposes of toxicology testing?
subject: subj:toxico

body.front: Purposes of toxicology testing?
body.back: Product safety, maximum tolerated dose, target organs, altered functions, genotoxic/carcinogenic risk, risk of congenital malformations.

title: Four sources of risk data?
subject: subj:toxico

body.front: Four sources of risk data?
body.back: Epidemiological, in vivo (animal), in vitro (cells, molecular), in silico (computer).

title: Design of a single-dose study?
subject: subj:toxico

body.front: Design of a single-dose study?
body.back: Rodents, both sexes, ~5/sex/dose, route as in humans, vehicle control, 14-day observation, necropsy; outputs LD₅₀/MTD, target organs, reversibility.

title: Factors influencing LD₅₀?
subject: subj:toxico

body.front: Factors influencing LD₅₀?
body.back: Species, strain, sex, age, weight/nutrition, route, first-pass, metabolic rate, chemical form, environment, vehicle.

title: Repeated-dose study durations and doses?
subject: subj:toxico

body.front: Repeated-dose study durations and doses?
body.back: Subacute 28 d, subchronic 90 d, chronic ≥ 6 months; three dose levels (no, mild, clear non-lethal toxicity) plus control.

title: NOEL, NOAEL, LOAEL?
subject: subj:toxico

body.front: NOEL, NOAEL, LOAEL?
body.back: NOEL: no observed effect. NOAEL: no observed adverse effect. LOAEL: lowest dose with an adverse effect.

title: Standard genotoxicity battery?
subject: subj:toxico

body.front: Standard genotoxicity battery?
body.back: Ames test, in vitro mammalian cell assay (e.g. chromosomal aberration), in vivo micronucleus test; transgenic mice to confirm.

title: Explain the Ames test.
subject: subj:toxico

body.front: Explain the Ames test.
body.back: Histidine-requiring Salmonella on histidine-free medium, with and without S9; more revertant colonies than control = mutagenic.

title: IARC classification?
subject: subj:toxico

body.front: IARC classification?
body.back: 1 carcinogenic, 2A probably, 2B possibly, 3 not classifiable, 4 probably not (caprolactam).

title: Reproductive toxicity study types?
subject: subj:toxico

body.front: Reproductive toxicity study types?
body.back: Fertility and early embryonic development, embryo-fetal development (teratogenicity), pre/postnatal development, multigeneration studies.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:toxico

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Benzodiazepines. Act on the GABA receptor, like barbiturates and ethanol.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:toxico

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Carbon monoxide. Binds haemoglobin 210 times more than oxygen, forming carboxyhaemoglobin.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:toxico

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Action on nucleic acids. Alkylating agents bind DNA, causing mutations and cancer.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:toxico

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Immunoallergic action. PPD in 'black henna' causes contact dermatitis; ingestion is often fatal.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:toxico

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Action on lipids. Lipid peroxidation by free radicals (paraquat, paracetamol, benzene).

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:toxico

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Non-specific action. Physical or chemical: asphyxiant gases (butane), surfactants, hydrocarbons, acids and alkalis.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:toxico

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Organophosphates. Inhibit acetylcholinesterase: cholinergic toxidrome; pralidoxime reactivates the enzyme.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:toxico

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Action on proteins. The commonest mechanism: enzymes, transport proteins or receptors.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:toxico

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Absence of a toxicant. Withdrawal syndromes after stopping opioids, tobacco or benzodiazepines.

title: Define toxicology.
subject: subj:toxico

body.front: Define toxicology.
body.back: The science of toxicants, toxins and poisons: their properties, harmful effects, mode of action, analysis in different matrices and treatment.

title: Toxicant, toxin, poison: differences?
subject: subj:toxico

body.front: Toxicant, toxin, poison: differences?
body.back: Toxicant: synthetic (pesticides). Toxin: natural (mushrooms, venoms). Poison: synonym used for criminal or suicidal intent.

title: List the branches of toxicology.
subject: subj:toxico

body.front: List the branches of toxicology.
body.back: Forensic, food safety, occupational, addictology, ecotoxicology, regulatory, biotoxicology, analytical.

title: Functional vs morphological toxicants with examples?
subject: subj:toxico

body.front: Functional vs morphological toxicants with examples?
body.back: Functional: blood level parallels severity (morphine, atropine, barbiturates, organophosphates). Morphological: structural damage, delayed, silent start (paracetamol liver, paraquat lung).

title: Acid vs alkali caustic injury?
subject: subj:toxico

body.front: Acid vs alkali caustic injury?
body.back: Acids: coagulative necrosis with eschar, more superficial. Alkalis: liquefactive necrosis, deeper and more extensive.

title: Carboxyhaemoglobin levels and effects?
subject: subj:toxico

body.front: Carboxyhaemoglobin levels and effects?
body.back: < 1.6% normal; smokers 3-5%; 20-30% headache, nausea, dizziness; 40-50% syncope, tachypnoea; 50-60% convulsions; 60-70% fatal.

title: Why is CO poisoning hard to diagnose?
subject: subj:toxico

body.front: Why is CO poisoning hard to diagnose?
body.back: Symptoms are variable and nonspecific; it mimics food poisoning (collective), flu (winter), neurovascular or psychiatric illness.

title: PPD poisoning: phases?
subject: subj:toxico

body.front: PPD poisoning: phases?
body.back: 2-3 h: burning mouth, vomiting, cervicofacial/angio-oedema, macroglossia, asphyxia. Then rhabdomyolysis, dark urine, acute renal failure, methaemoglobinaemia; 20-90% fatal.

title: Consequences of endocrine disruptors?
subject: subj:toxico

body.front: Consequences of endocrine disruptors?
body.back: Female: precocious puberty, PCOS, endometriosis, miscarriage. Male: testicular dysgenesis, hypospadias, cryptorchidism, poor sperm. Hormone-dependent cancers, metabolic disorders.

title: Factors modulating toxicity?
subject: subj:toxico

body.front: Factors modulating toxicity?
body.back: Substance (route, speed, concentration, solubility, volatility, vehicle, metabolism), organism (age, sex, pregnancy, organ failure, fasting), environment, tolerance, interactions.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:toxico

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Absorption. Crossing membranes into blood, mainly by passive diffusion (Fick's law); bioavailability F.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:toxico

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Distribution. Plasma protein binding, ion trapping, organ blood flow and tropism, BBB and placenta; volume of distribution.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:toxico

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Excretion. Urine (filtration, secretion, reabsorption), bile, lungs, milk, saliva, sweat, hair.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:toxico

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Metabolism. Phase I functionalisation by CYP450 (may create toxic metabolites) and phase II conjugation.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:toxico

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Kinetic parameters. Half-life, clearance, first- vs zero-order kinetics, steady state after 4-5 half-lives.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:toxico

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Post-mortem redistribution. After death, lipophilic drugs diffuse from tissues into central blood: sample femoral blood.

title: Define toxicokinetics.
subject: subj:toxico

body.front: Define toxicokinetics.
body.back: What the body does to a toxicant: absorption, distribution, metabolism and excretion (ADME), with patient/disease factors and mathematical modelling.

title: Five mechanisms of membrane passage?
subject: subj:toxico

body.front: Five mechanisms of membrane passage?
body.back: Passive diffusion (main), facilitated diffusion, active transport, filtration through pores, endocytosis (pinocytosis, phagocytosis).

title: SLC vs ABC transporters?
subject: subj:toxico

body.front: SLC vs ABC transporters?
body.back: SLC (OATP, OCT, PEPT): bring substances into cells. ABC (P-gp, BCRP, MRP): pump them out, protecting brain, liver, kidney, gut.

title: How does pH affect oral absorption?
subject: subj:toxico

body.front: How does pH affect oral absorption?
body.back: Only the un-ionised form crosses; acids are un-ionised at low pH, bases at high pH.

title: Consequences of plasma protein binding?
subject: subj:toxico

body.front: Consequences of plasma protein binding?
body.back: Maintains absorption gradient, reduces filtration and metabolism; lowers immediate toxicity but prolongs intoxication.

title: Phase I vs phase II metabolism?
subject: subj:toxico

body.front: Phase I vs phase II metabolism?
body.back: Phase I: CYP oxidation, reduction, hydrolysis; adds functional groups; may create toxic metabolites. Phase II: glucuronidation, sulfation, acetylation, glutathione; makes products excretable.

title: Three renal excretion steps?
subject: subj:toxico

body.front: Three renal excretion steps?
body.back: Glomerular filtration (small unbound molecules), active tubular secretion (proximal), passive tubular reabsorption (pH-dependent).

title: Minor excretion routes and their uses?
subject: subj:toxico

body.front: Minor excretion routes and their uses?
body.back: Lungs (breathalyser), milk (infant exposure), saliva and sweat (drug tests), hair (retrospective calendar), meconium (in-utero exposure).

title: First-order vs zero-order kinetics?
subject: subj:toxico

body.front: First-order vs zero-order kinetics?
body.back: First-order: constant fraction removed per time (most drugs). Zero-order: constant amount per time (alcohol, high-dose aspirin), risk of accumulation.

title: How do you limit post-mortem redistribution errors?
subject: subj:toxico

body.front: How do you limit post-mortem redistribution errors?
body.back: Sample femoral blood, compare vitreous humour and liver, consider the post-mortem interval and the case context.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:toxico

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Toxic acidosis. High anion gap: methanol, ethylene glycol, salicylates, iron, metformin, cyanide, CO. Normal gap: toluene, acetazolamide.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:toxico

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Coagulation. Hypocoagulation (warfarin, rodenticides, liver toxins), hypercoagulation (oestrogens, chemotherapy), DIC (sepsis, venoms).

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:toxico

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Haemoglobin disorders. Methaemoglobin (Fe³⁺, chocolate blood, methylene blue) and carboxyhaemoglobin (CO, oxygen).

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:toxico

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Erythrocyte toxicity. Microcytic (lead), megaloblastic (methotrexate, N₂O, alcohol), haemolytic (G6PD deficiency, venoms).

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:toxico

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Toxic rhabdomyolysis. Muscle breakdown releasing myoglobin, CK and potassium; cocaine, statins, PPD; risk of acute kidney injury.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:toxico

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: White cells and platelets. Leukopenia, agranulocytosis (clozapine), thrombocytopenia (heparin), platelet dysfunction (aspirin), pancytopenia (benzene, chloramphenicol).

title: Methaemoglobinaemia: mechanism, causes, signs?
subject: subj:toxico

body.front: Methaemoglobinaemia: mechanism, causes, signs?
body.back: Fe²⁺ oxidised to Fe³⁺, no O₂ binding. Dapsone, benzocaine, lidocaine, nitrates/nitrites, sulphonamides, aniline, nitrobenzene. Cyanosis unresponsive to O₂, chocolate blood, SpO₂ ≈ 85%.

title: Treatment of methaemoglobinaemia?
subject: subj:toxico

body.front: Treatment of methaemoglobinaemia?
body.back: Methylene blue 1-2 mg/kg IV over 5 min (not in G6PD deficiency); oxygen; vitamin C, exchange transfusion or hyperbaric O₂ if refractory.

title: CO vs MetHb on pulse oximetry and blood colour?
subject: subj:toxico

body.front: CO vs MetHb on pulse oximetry and blood colour?
body.back: CO: SpO₂ falsely normal, cherry red. MetHb: SpO₂ falsely low (~85%), chocolate brown. Both confirmed by co-oximetry.

title: Indications for hyperbaric oxygen in CO poisoning?
subject: subj:toxico

body.front: Indications for hyperbaric oxygen in CO poisoning?
body.back: COHb > 25% (> 15% in pregnancy), neurological symptoms, cardiac ischaemia.

title: Toxic causes of megaloblastic anaemia?
subject: subj:toxico

body.front: Toxic causes of megaloblastic anaemia?
body.back: Methotrexate, trimethoprim, phenytoin (folate); alcohol, nitrous oxide (B12); hydroxyurea, zidovudine; alcohol directly.

title: G6PD deficiency haemolysis: triggers and labs?
subject: subj:toxico

body.front: G6PD deficiency haemolysis: triggers and labs?
body.back: Dapsone, sulphonamides, nitrofurantoin, primaquine, high-dose aspirin, fava beans, infection, naphthalene. Low Hb, high reticulocytes, LDH, indirect bilirubin, low haptoglobin, bite cells, Heinz bodies.

title: Toxic causes of pancytopenia?
subject: subj:toxico

body.front: Toxic causes of pancytopenia?
body.back: Chemotherapy, chloramphenicol, NSAIDs (rare), antithyroid drugs, antiepileptics, gold salts, benzene, pesticides, radiation.

title: Lab pattern of DIC?
subject: subj:toxico

body.front: Lab pattern of DIC?
body.back: High PT/INR and aPTT, low platelets, low fibrinogen, very high D-dimers.

title: Toxic causes of high anion gap acidosis?
subject: subj:toxico

body.front: Toxic causes of high anion gap acidosis?
body.back: Methanol, ethylene glycol, salicylates, iron, isoniazid, metformin, cyanide, CO, arsenic.

title: Rhabdomyolysis: releases, signs, complications?
subject: subj:toxico

body.front: Rhabdomyolysis: releases, signs, complications?
body.back: Myoglobin, CK, K⁺, phosphate, uric acid. Pain, weakness, cola urine, CK > 5×. AKI (ATN), hyperkalaemia, hypocalcaemia, arrhythmias, DIC, compartment syndrome.
